items.text: WTI and Brent crude surged 9.6% and 8.8% week-over-week respectively to $91.48 and $96.02, reflecting geopolitical risk and supply tightness. For credit investors, elevated energy prices threaten margins in transportation, shipping, and dependent supply chains while supporting energy-linked corporates and benefiting firms with hedges already in place.

ISM Manufacturing employment eased to 51.2 in August from 52.8 in July, signaling softer job creation despite eight consecutive months of manufacturing expansion. Unemployment remains stable at 4.1%, but weakening labor dynamics in manufacturing and ISM Services employment at 47.8 (vs. 51.8 expected) suggest cooling demand for new hires—a mixed signal ahead of potential policy shifts.

Producer-level cost pressures strengthened in China with input costs rising at their fastest pace in three months, while output prices returned to growth. US headline CPI at 3.3% (down from 3.46%) and core at 2.47% (down from 2.57%) show deceleration, but consumer one-year inflation expectations rose to 4.3% in early August, indicating unanchored long-term sentiment despite near-term disinflation.

ECB deposit rate is at 2.25% with market pricing implying a 99% probability of a 25bp increase to 2.50% at the September 10 meeting, signaling continued euro-area tightening despite soft demand. Fed funds remain at 3.75%, and the 2-10 curve at 40bp is flat—compressed terminal rates reflect policy divergence and growing recession risk if global growth slows further.

HY OAS widened 2bp to 267bp while IG OAS was flat at 81bp and CCC-rated OAS jumped 5bp to 1056bp, suggesting risk-off in lower-rated credits. Manufacturers cited rising costs, supply-chain disruptions, tariff uncertainty and geopolitical tension, with the Prices Index remaining elevated at 71.1—pressuring leveraged borrowers reliant on pass-through or margin absorption.

ISM Manufacturing PMI rose to 55.6 in July, the strongest expansion since May 2022, but eased to 54.6 in August below the 55.2 consensus, with new orders slowing sharply to 53.7 from 56.7. Services PMI at 55.4 in August, up 1.3 points from July, provides some offset. Momentum is moderating after a sharp summer rebound, raising questions about sustainability into Q4.

University of Michigan consumer sentiment fell to 51.7 in August from 55.2 in July, down roughly 6% and 11% below year-ago, reflecting persistent inflation worries and geopolitical uncertainty. Sentiment is at the 1st percentile of historical distribution, but housing data lags (through July); mortgage rates at 6.71% continue to weigh on affordability and transaction volume.

themeCards.title: Oil price shock & geopolitical risk
themeCards.statusLine: WTI +9.6% to $91.48, Brent +8.8% to $96 in a week; Iran tensions and Middle East supply uncertainty driving spike. Pass-through risk for refiners, transporters, and energy-intensive sectors.
themeCards.relevance: Leveraged corporates in transport, logistics, and chemicals face near-term margin compression. Hedged energy producers benefit; unhedged operationals distressed. Credit spreads may not yet price full earnings impact if crude stays elevated.

themeCards.title: China growth divergence & stimulus void
themeCards.statusLine: Official PMI 49.8 (contraction), but high-tech sub-index at 52.9 showing AI-driven bifurcation. Small firms at 47.9, large at 50.6—policy support for SOEs masks SME weakness and consumer malaise.
themeCards.relevance: Global supply chains and offshore credit exposure face uneven demand. Chinese credit issuers (esp. property, SME-exposed financials) at risk if stimulus remains inadequate; bifurcation creates winners/losers among multinationals and exporters.

themeCards.title: US consumer sentiment collapse
themeCards.statusLine: Sentiment at 51.7, the 1st percentile of historical distribution; driven by inflation angst and policy uncertainty. Notably weak among Republicans, older cohorts, and lower-income groups—the least able to absorb cost increases.
themeCards.relevance: Default risk tilts toward consumer discretionary credit and leveraged retail; tight budget consumers may curtail spending, pressuring retail margins and reducing refinance ability for weak credits. High-yield consumer issuers face refinancing risk if sentiment stays depressed.

themeCards.title: Manufacturing demand momentum fade
themeCards.statusLine: ISM Mfg new orders slowed sharply from 56.7 to 53.7; backlogs down 3.2 points to 51.8. Services new orders also flat-to-soft. Expansion is 8 months old; leading indicators suggest peak-to-contraction may be approaching.
themeCards.relevance: Industrial credit and capex-funded corporates face demand erosion; backlog normalization leaves less cushion for order books. Equipment financiers and supply-chain lenders should watch for refinancing pressure if volumes soften further.

themeCards.title: Subordinated credit & leverage stress
themeCards.statusLine: CCC OAS jumped 5bp to 1056bp while IG steady; cost-push (tariffs, supply chain, energy) paired with softer demand threatens highly leveraged structures. Covenant creep and PIK toggle strategies under pressure.
themeCards.relevance: CCC/B credits and leveraged lending exposed to covenant breach as EBITDA declines. Opportunistic distressed/special situations may emerge if credit events spike; watch LBO sponsors for forced asset sales.

ecb.delta: 99% market odds of +25bp at Sept 10 meeting

chinaPMI.delta: up 0.6 from 49.2 in July, but still in contraction for 2nd month

ismServices.delta: up 1.3 from 54.1 in July, strongest since Feb; new orders surged to 60.9

regime.label: Mid-to-late cycle
regime.detail: Manufacturing peak momentum, services resilient but labor cooling; inflation moderating headline but consumer expectations unanchored; policy tightening abroad (ECB hike likely), US rates hold; credit spreads bifurcated—IG tight, CCC under stress.
